design_rationale: The study explicitly used 1:1 allocation according to a computer-generated randomization schedule, with assignments placed in sequentially numbered, opaque, sealed envelopes.

domain_judgments.rationale: The allocation sequence was computer-generated and concealed in sequentially numbered, opaque, sealed envelopes opened by a clinician independent of the study, and the reported baseline characteristics were broadly balanced.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Neonates with clinical seizures were randomly assigned to receive either PB or LEV with a 1:1 allocation as per a computer-generated randomization schedule and using sequentially numbered, opaque and sealed envelopes. When an eligible neonate was eligible to be enrolled, the envelope was opened by a clinician who was not part of the study.

domain_judgments.rationale: The trial was open-label, so treating clinicians knew allocation and could potentially influence co-interventions or clinical management, while the report does not explicitly describe an intention-to-treat analysis, although all randomized participants appear included in the primary analysis.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Design: Open labelled, Randomized controlled trial.

domain_judgments.rationale: Primary seizure outcomes and acute adverse events were reported for all 100 randomized neonates, with 50 analyzed in each group; later losses, discharge, and death occurred after the 24-hour primary endpoint.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: In the LEV group, there was a cessation of clinical seizures (and remaining seizure free at 24 h) in 43 (86%), and in the PB group, it was 31 (62%) after one or two doses.

domain_judgments.rationale: Seizure cessation was assessed clinically without electroencephalographic confirmation in an open-label trial, making this partly subjective primary outcome vulnerable to differential ascertainment by assessors aware of treatment assignment.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: The limitation of our study was that we did not perform electroencephalographic monitoring to document cessation of seizure activity.

domain_judgments.rationale: Although a trial registration is cited and the primary and secondary outcomes are defined, registration occurred in April 2018 after recruitment ended in April 2016, so prospective specification cannot be established and selective reporting remains possible.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Trial Registration: Clinical Trial Registry of India (CTRI/2018/04/013161).

overall_summary: Overall risk of bias is high, driven by clinical assessment of seizure cessation without EEG confirmation in an open-label trial, which could make outcome ascertainment depend on knowledge of treatment. There are also some concerns about deviations in the unblinded setting and selective reporting because the trial registration appears retrospective.

design_rationale: The study explicitly used computer-generated block randomization, with assignments placed in serially numbered opaque sealed envelopes prepared by a person not involved in the study.

domain_judgments.rationale: Computer-generated block randomization and opaque sealed envelopes indicate an appropriate concealed process, and measured baseline characteristics were similar, but the unexplained 42:38 allocation is inconsistent with a straightforward balanced block size of four across 80 participants.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Block randomization of 80 numbers in blocks of four was done using computer generated random numbers. They were put in serially numbered opaque envelopes and sealed. This was done by a person not involved in study.

domain_judgments.rationale: The trial was open-label, allowing care decisions to be influenced by assignment, and treatment included protocol-defined crossover and third-line therapy; although intention-to-treat analysis was stated, the report does not establish that all deviations were balanced or appropriately handled for every outcome.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Our trial was an open-label trial, so the doctors and nursing staff were aware of the treatment assignments.

domain_judgments.rationale: The 12-month outcomes were available for only 48 of 80 randomized neonates because 18 died and 14 of 62 survivors were lost to follow-up, with no analysis demonstrating that missing outcomes could not depend on outcome status; the reported long-term comparison therefore risks substantial attrition bias.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Among 62 discharged babies, 14 were lost to follow-up, and 48 babies (25 babies in LEV group and 23 babies in PB group) were followed at 3 months, 6 months, and 12 months.

domain_judgments.rationale: The primary seizure outcome was based on unblinded clinical observation without bedside EEG, and long-term outcomes mixed in-person standardized assessments with less reliable unblinded telephone reports, so measurement could differ or be influenced by treatment knowledge.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Lack of blinding of clinical outcomes, inability to monitor serum drug level and cerebral function, small sample size, and unavailability of bedside EEG were the limitation of our study.

domain_judgments.rationale: No protocol or prespecified statistical analysis plan is reported, while several outcomes, time points, and possible analyses were available, leaving scope for selective reporting despite the outcomes being listed in the Methods.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: The primary outcome variable was cessation of clinical seizure activity (no seizure for 5 days). Secondary outcome variables were time taken to control seizures, survival at discharge, shortterm adverse effect and long-term neurodevelopmental outcome at 12 months (Amiel-Tison method), and EEG control of seizures.

overall_summary: Overall risk of bias is high, driven by substantial missing 12-month outcome data and high risk in outcome measurement due to unblinded clinical seizure assessment, lack of bedside EEG, and mixed in-person/telephone developmental follow-up. Additional concerns arise from the allocation imbalance, open-label care, and absence of a reported protocol or analysis plan.

design_rationale: The study explicitly states that 44 participants were randomly allocated to probiotic soy milk or conventional soy milk, so RoB 2 applies.

domain_judgments.rationale: Although allocation was described as random and most baseline measures were similar, the sequence-generation and allocation-concealment methods were not reported, and carbohydrate intake showed a notable baseline imbalance.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: A total of 44 participants were randomly allocated to the soy milk group (control) or probiotic soy milk group... However, dietary carbohydrate intake was significantly higher in the control group (P < .001) compared with the probiotic soy milk group.

domain_judgments.rationale: The trial was described as double-blind and adherence was actively monitored, but who was blinded and how blinding was maintained were not detailed, and the complete-case analysis excluded four randomized participants rather than clearly using intention-to-treat.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: At each study visit, participants received sufficient bottles of soy milk for a 3-day period until the next visit, in a doubleblinded design... Forty-four patients participated, and 40 completed the study (20 patients in each group).

domain_judgments.rationale: Outcome data were missing for 4 of 44 randomized participants (9.1%), with balanced attrition but one exclusion for poor adherence and no sensitivity analysis demonstrating that missingness could not bias the findings.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Two men in the probiotic group were excluded because of hospitalization (n = 1) and loss to follow-up (n = 1). One man and 1 woman in the control group were also excluded due to poor adherence and loss to follow-up.

domain_judgments.rationale: Kidney and biomarker outcomes were measured with objective laboratory methods applied identically across groups, with samples analyzed blinded, paired, in the same run, and in random order.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: All the tests were performed in a blinded fashion, in pairs (before and after the intervention) at the same time, in the same analytic run, and in random order to reduce systematic error and interassay variability.

domain_judgments.rationale: The trial was registered and primary endpoints were identified, but the provided report does not establish that registration or a prespecified analysis plan preceded enrollment, and multiple endpoints and analytic approaches leave some potential for selective reporting.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: The study protocol was registered at the Iranian Registry of Clinical Trials (Register code: IRCT201601027479N2 available at: http://www.irct.ir).

overall_summary: Overall risk of bias is some concerns. The main issues are absent details on sequence generation and allocation concealment, incomplete specification of blinding, complete-case rather than clearly intention-to-treat analysis with 9% attrition, and residual uncertainty about prespecification; objective blinded outcome measurement is a strength.

design_rationale: The study explicitly states that the 30 term neonates were randomly assigned to receive phenobarbital or levetiracetam, although the method used to generate the allocation sequence is not described.

domain_judgments.rationale: Random assignment is stated, but the sequence-generation method and allocation concealment are not reported; measured baseline scores were similar, although the very small groups leave uncertainty about balance in prognostic factors such as seizure etiology.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Newborns were randomly assigned to receive PB and LEV in a blinded manner.

domain_judgments.rationale: The study is described as one-blind and treatment was reportedly administered in a blinded manner, but who was blinded is unclear, the visibly different dosing protocols could reveal assignment, and no intention-to-treat analysis or protocol-deviation information is reported.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: This was a randomized, one-blind prospective study conducted on term newborns receiving PB or LEV as first-line treatment for seizure control.

domain_judgments.rationale: All 30 randomized neonates appear in the two 15-participant groups and both baseline and one-month outcome summaries are reported, with no losses to follow-up or missing outcome observations indicated.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: We included 30 neonates, 12 females and 18 males

domain_judgments.rationale: HNNE is an appropriate standardized measure applied at both time points, but assessor blinding is not clearly stated, the treatment regimens could disclose allocation, and the reported analysis primarily tests within-group change rather than directly comparing change between randomized groups, making the claimed comparative effect vulnerable to measurement and analysis bias.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: The Hammersmith score was evaluated by trained neonatologists of our NICU

domain_judgments.rationale: No prospective registration, protocol, or prespecified analysis plan is reported, multiple HNNE domains and time-point contrasts were tested, and the conclusions rely on significance within the LEV group versus nonsignificance within the PB group rather than a prespecified between-group treatment-effect test, creating substantial scope for selective analysis and reporting.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: The Student t-test was used to compare quantitative results.

overall_summary: Overall risk of bias is high, driven by unclear randomization/concealment and blinding, and especially by the absence of a prespecified analysis plan coupled with selective emphasis on within-group significance rather than a valid direct randomized-group comparison. Outcome completeness appears good, but it does not offset the high-risk measurement/analysis and reporting concerns.

design_rationale: The Methods explicitly state that eligible neonates were assigned by a simple random lottery method with replacement to levetiracetam or phenobarbitone.

domain_judgments.rationale: A random lottery method was reported and measured baseline characteristics were generally similar, but allocation concealment and implementation safeguards were not described, and the unusual use of replacement leaves some uncertainty about sequence integrity.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: After necessary exclusion and inclusion criteria randomization was done by simple random method; i.e.by lottery method with replacement.

domain_judgments.rationale: The trial appears open-label, no blinding or intention-to-treat analysis is described, and post-failure treatment followed institutional protocol, although all 100 randomized neonates appear to have been analyzed in their assigned groups for the main outcome.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Decision regarding further for treatment in case of treatment failure was made on the basis of institutional treatment protocol.

domain_judgments.rationale: The principal seizure-control outcome is reported for all 50 neonates in each randomized group, with no indicated missing outcome observations.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Seizure of 33 (66%) neonates of intervention group was controlled with inj. Levetiracetam and 19 (38%) neonates of control group was controlled with inj. Phenobarbitone.

domain_judgments.rationale: Seizure cessation was assessed clinically without continuous EEG in an apparently unblinded comparison, so the subjective primary outcome could be differentially misclassified by observers aware of treatment assignment.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Seizures were diagnosed clinically. No continuous EEG monitoring was performed at time of diagnosis and enrolment.

domain_judgments.rationale: No protocol, trial registration, or prespecified statistical analysis plan is reported, while several outcomes and representations of seizure control and timing were analyzed, leaving scope for selective reporting.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: The outcome variables were seizure control, times taken to be seizure free, and hospital stay.

overall_summary: Overall risk of bias is high because the clinically assessed seizure outcome was measured without continuous EEG and apparently without blinded assessors, creating substantial potential for differential outcome misclassification. Additional concerns arise from unreported allocation concealment, absence of a stated intention-to-treat analysis, and no reported protocol or prespecified analysis plan.

design_rationale: The study explicitly reports computer-generated random allocation of 60 eligible neonates to levetiracetam or phenobarbitone, with assignment concealed in serially numbered opaque sealed envelopes opened by an independent worker.

domain_judgments.rationale: The allocation sequence was computer generated, concealment used serially numbered opaque sealed envelopes opened only after enrollment by an independent worker, and reported baseline characteristics were comparable.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Randomization was done using computer generated numbers. Labelled slips were put in serially numbered opaque and sealed envelopes. They were opened when an eligible baby was enrolled by an independent worker, not worked in the study.

domain_judgments.rationale: Clinical staff were unblinded in this open-label trial, which could influence co-interventions or decisions about clinically observed seizure control, although treatment protocols were specified and the analysis was reported as intention-to-treat.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: The team members managing the babies were aware of the treatment allocation... It was done using intention to treat analysis on SPSS 10.

domain_judgments.rationale: The primary outcome of clinical seizure control was reported for all 60 randomized neonates, with denominators of 30 in each group.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Clinically apparent seizures were controlled in only 7 of the 30 (23.3%) neonates assigned to receive levetiracetam as compared to 26 of the 30 (86.7%) neonates assigned to receive phenobarbitone.

domain_judgments.rationale: The primary outcome was based on clinical observation rather than continuous EEG, and the unblinded team managing the neonates could therefore have been influenced by treatment knowledge when judging seizure control; the authors also acknowledge that clinical assessment misses many electrical seizures.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: The team members managing the babies were aware of the treatment allocation... Also, we did not do cerebral function or continuous EEG monitoring. So electrical seizures could still be persisting despite clinical control of seizures.

domain_judgments.rationale: No prospective registration, protocol, or prespecified statistical analysis plan is reported, and several outcomes and time points were analyzed, leaving potential for selective reporting despite clear identification of the primary outcome in the article.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: Clinical control of seizure activity was the primary outcome variable of this study... Secondary outcomes were safety profile of levetiracetam, electrical seizures after control of clinical seizure, time taken to control seizures, and neurological examination till 6 months.

overall_summary: Overall risk of bias is high, driven chiefly by the clinically assessed primary outcome being judged in an open-label setting without continuous EEG confirmation. There are also some concerns about possible deviations associated with unblinded care and selective reporting in the absence of a reported protocol or registration.
